parole.testo: From Late Latin -archa, from Latin -archēs, from Ancient Greek -άρχης (-árkhēs), from ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “rule”, “government”).

parole.significato: used to form verbs from adjectives or nouns
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin -izāre. Doublet of -izzare, which was borrowed. Cognate with Sicilian -ijari.
From Late Latin or Ecclesiastical Latin abbātia, derived from Latin abbās (“abbot”), from Ancient Greek ἀββᾶς (abbâs), from Aramaic אבא (’abbā, “father”). Compare Sicilian batìa.
Borrowed from Late Latin abyssus, from Ancient Greek ἄβῠσσος (ábŭssos, “bottomless”).
Borrowed from Late Latin acatalēctus, from Ancient Greek ἀκατάληκτος (akatálēktos, “leaving off”).
From Late Latin acolythus, from Ancient Greek ἀκόλουθος (akólouthos, “follower, attendant”).
Borrowed from Late Latin acēdia, from Ancient Greek ἀκηδίᾱ (akēdíā, “negligence”). Doublet of accidia.
Borrowed from Late Latin acherontēus, from Ancient Greek Ἀχερόντειος (Akherónteios).
Borrowed from Late Latin aphaeresis, from Ancient Greek ἀφαίρεσις (aphaíresis), derived from Ancient Greek ἀφαιρέω (aphairéō, “I remove”).
From Late Latin aphorismus, from Ancient Greek ἀφορισμός (aphorismós, “pithy phrase containing a general truth”).
From Late Latin adiectīvum [nōmen], translation of Ancient Greek ἐπίθετον [ὄνομα] (epítheton [ónoma]).

Borrowed from Late Latin alphabētum, from Ancient Greek ἀλφάβητος (alphábētos), from alpha and beta (the first two letters of the Greek alphabet), from Phoenician 𐤀 (ʾ /⁠aleph⁠/, “ox”) and 𐤁 (b /⁠beth⁠/, “house”), so called because they were pictograms of those objects.
From Late Latin ambōnem, from Ancient Greek ἄμβων (ámbōn).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin anacoluthon, from Ancient Greek ἀνακόλουθον (anakólouthon).
From Late Latin anachoreta, from Ancient Greek ἀναχωρητής (anakhōrētḗs).
Borrowed from Late Latin anaglyphus, from Ancient Greek ἀνάγλυφος (anágluphos).
From Late Latin anathema, from Ancient Greek ἀνάθεμα (anáthema).
From Late Latin anōmalus, anōmalos, from Ancient Greek ἀνώμαλος (anṓmalos, “uneven, irregular”).
From Late Latin anōnymus, from Ancient Greek ἀνώνυμος (anṓnumos, “without name”), from ἀν- (an-, “without”) + ὄνυμα (ónuma, “name”).

parole.significato: a person living on the same latitude, but in the opposite hemisphere
parole.testo: From Late Latin antoecus, from Ancient Greek ἄντοικος (ántoikos).
From Late Latin antichresis, from Ancient Greek ἀντίχρησις (antíkhrēsis).
From Late Latin antiphrasis, from Ancient Greek ἀντίφρασις (antíphrasis).
Borrowed from Late Latin antistrophe, antistropha, from Ancient Greek ἀντιστροφή (antistrophḗ, “turning about”). By surface analysis, anti- + strofe.
Borrowed from Late Latin antitheticus, from Ancient Greek ἀντιθετικός (antithetikós). By surface analysis, antiteto (“antithet”) + -ico (“-ical, pertaining to”).
Borrowed from Late Latin apēliōtēs, from Ancient Greek ἀπηλιώτης (apēliṓtēs), compound of ἀπό (apó, “from”) + ἥλιος (hḗlios, “sun”).
Borrowed from Late Latin apyrĕtus, from Ancient Greek ἀπύρετος (apúretos), from ἀ- (a-) + πυρετός (puretós). By surface analysis, a- + piretico.
Borrowed from Late Latin apostata, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀποστάτης (apostátēs).
From Late Latin apostolus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόστολος (apóstolos, “messenger, one sent forth”), from ἀποστέλλω (apostéllō, “to send off”), from ἀπό (apó, “from”) + στέλλω (stéllō, “to set”).

parole.significato: apostrophe (sudden piece of dialogue addressed to someone or something)
parole.testo: From Late Latin apostrophe, from Ancient Greek ἀποστροφή (apostrophḗ, literally “a turning away”), from ἀποστρέφω (apostréphō, literally “I turn away”).
From Late Latin apostrophus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόστροφος (apóstrophos, literally “turned backwards”), from ἀποστρέφω (apostréphō, literally “I turn away”).
Borrowed from Late Latin apozema, from Ancient Greek ἀπόζεμα (apózema). Doublet of bozzima.
From Late Latin, from Ancient Greek ἀρχαϊσμός (arkhaïsmós). By surface analysis, arcaico + -ismo.
From arci- + diacono, a calque of Late Latin archidiaconus, which in turn derives from Ancient Greek ἀρχιδιάκονος (arkhidiákonos).
From arci- + vescovo; modeled on Late Latin archiepiscopus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχιεπίσκοπος (arkhiepískopos), from ἀρχι- (arkhi-, “first, chief”) + ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos, “overseer”).
Borrowed from Late Latin arnoglossa, from Ancient Greek ἀρνόγλωσσον (arnóglōsson, literally “lamb's tongue”).
Borrowed from Late Latin ascēta, from Ancient Greek ἀσκητής (askētḗs).
From Late Latin asphaltum, from Ancient Greek ἄσφαλτος (ásphaltos, “asphalt, bitumen”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin asteriscus, from Ancient Greek ἀστερίσκος (asterískos, “a little star, asterisk, used in manuscripts to mark passages”).
Borrowed from Late Latin athērōma (“tumor full of gruel-like matter”), from Ancient Greek ἀθήρωμα (athḗrōma, “tumor”).
From Late Latin ballistra, from ballista, Ancient Greek βαλλίστρα (ballístra).
Uncertain. Various theories exist. One ties it to Late Latin *ballizāre, from Ancient Greek βαλλίζω (ballízō). Another derives it from Late Latin balteāre, from baltea, from Latin balteus (“belt”).
From Late Latin basaltes, a misspelling of Latin basanites, from Ancient Greek βασανίτης (basanítēs), from βάσανος (básanos, “touchstone”), from Egyptian b-x:n-O39 (bḫn, “a hard stone”).
Borrowed from Late Latin batus, from Ancient Greek βάτος (bátos), from Biblical Hebrew בַּת (bat).

parole.significato: Bethlehemite (of, from or relating to Bethlehem)
parole.testo: From Late Latin bēthlehemītēs, from Ancient Greek Βηθλεεμίτης (Bēthleemítēs). By surface analysis, Betlem(me) (“Bethlehem”) + -ita (“-ite”).
From Late Latin bigămus, from Ancient Greek δίγαμος (dígamos), with the Latinate prefix bi- replacing Hellenic di-.
From Late Latin blasphēmia, from Ancient Greek βλασφημία (blasphēmía, “slander, blasphemy”).
From Late Latin blasphēmus, from Ancient Greek βλάσφημος (blásphēmos).
From Late Latin bōca, from Ancient Greek βῶκα (bôka), from βοῦς (boûs, “ox”) + ὤψ (ṓps, “eye, view”).
From Late Latin bōlus (“clod of earth, lump”), from Ancient Greek βῶλος (bôlos, “clod, lump”).
From Late Latin buttis probably of Ancient Greek origin. Cognate with Sicilian vutti.
Borrowed from Late Latin bronchus, from Ancient Greek βρόγχος (brónkhos, “throat”).
Borrowed from Late Latin brūchus, from Ancient Greek βροῦκος (broûkos). Compare Portuguese bruco.
From Late Latin bufalus, from Latin būbalus, from Ancient Greek βούβαλος (boúbalos) "antelope, wild ox".
From Late Latin chalazion, from Ancient Greek χαλάζιον (khalázion), diminutive of χάλαζα (khálaza, “hail”).

Origin uncertain. Possibly from Late Latin cauma, from Ancient Greek καῦμα (kaûma, “heat, heat of the sun”). Compare Late Latin caumāre (“to rest during the heat (of the day), to siesta”), Sursilvan Romansh cauma (“resting place for livestock, especially during the noon heat”). If the Italian (and I
From Late Latin canapa, from Latin cannabis, from Ancient Greek κάνναβις (kánnabis); see there for more. Doublet of the borrowing cannabis. Compare Sicilian cànnavu and English canvas.

parole.significato: The name of the Latin script letter K/k.; kay
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin cappa, from Ancient Greek κάππα (káppa).
From Late Latin catalogus, from Ancient Greek κατάλογος (katálogos, “register, list”).
From Late Latin catarrhus, from Ancient Greek κατάρροος (katárrhoos, “catarrh, head cold”).

Learned borrowing from Late Latin catēchūmenus, from Ancient Greek κατηχούμενος (katēkhoúmenos, “being instructed”), present participle passive of κατηχέω (katēkhéō, “to sound through, instruct orally”).
Borrowed from Late Latin catēgoria, from Ancient Greek κατηγορία (katēgoría).
From Late Latin, Ecclesiastical Latin cathēdrālis, from Latin cathedra, from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra).
Borrowed from Late Latin cautērium, from Ancient Greek καυτήριον (kautḗrion).

parole.significato: melting pot, crucible (recipient where metals are melted)
parole.testo: From Late Latin cattia, perhaps from Ancient Greek κύαθος (kúathos, “ladle”).
Inherited from Late Latin cephalus, from Ancient Greek κέφαλος (képhalos), derived from κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”).
From Late Latin chīrurgicus (“surgical”, adjective), from Ancient Greek χειρουργικός (kheirourgikós). Doublet of chirurgico.
From Late Latin cherūb, from Ancient Greek χερούβ (kheroúb), ultimately from Biblical Hebrew כְּרוּב (kərūḇ).
From Late Latin chiasmus, from Ancient Greek χιασμός (khiasmós).
Inherited from Late Latin clēricus, from Ancient Greek κληρικός (klērikós, “of the clergy”).
Inherited from Late Latin glōssa, from Ancient Greek γλῶσσα (glôssa). Doublet of glossa.
From Late Latin cyclus (“cycle”), from Ancient Greek κύκλος (kúklos, “circle”).
From Late Latin cimelium, from Ancient Greek κειμήλιον (keimḗlion, “relic”).
From Late Latin coemeterium, Ancient Greek κοιμητήριον (koimētḗrion).

parole.significato: hunting (especially with the use of dogs)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin cynēgeticus, from Ancient Greek κυνηγετικός (kunēgetikós, “of or pertaining to hunting”).
Borrowed from Late Latin cinyra, from Ancient Greek κινύρᾱ (kinúrā), from Hebrew כינור (kinór, “lyre”).
From Late Latin citron, from Ancient Greek κίτρον (kítron), in turn from Latin citrum.
Borrowed from Late Latin clīma, from Ancient Greek κλῐ́μᾰ (klĭ́mă, “region, zone”), from κλῐ́νω (klĭ́nō, “to slope, incline”).
Inherited from Late Latin colpus, from Latin colaphus from Ancient Greek κόλαφος (kólaphos). Doublet of golfo.
Borrowed from Late Latin choriambĭcus, from Ancient Greek χοριαμβικός (khoriambikós). By surface analysis, coriambo + -ico.
From Late Latin choriambus, from Ancient Greek χορίαμβος (khoríambos).
Borrowed from Late Latin chorion, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek χόριον (khórion).
Inherited from Late Latin chrisma, from Ancient Greek χρῖσμα (khrîsma).
Borrowed from Late Latin chrisma, from Ancient Greek χρῖσμα (khrîsma).
From Late Latin Christianismus, from Christus, corresponding to Ancient Greek χρῑστιᾱνισμός (khrīstiānismós). By surface analysis, cristiano (“Christian”) + -esimo (“-ism”).

parole.significato: to Christianize, to convert to Christianity
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin chrīstiānizāre, from Ancient Greek χριστιανίζω (khristianízō). By surface analysis, cristiano + -izzare.

parole.significato: A line of verse containing ten syllables (in classical Italian verse)
parole.testo: From Late Latin decasyllabus, from Ancient Greek δεκασύλλαβος (dekasúllabos), from δέκᾰ (dékă, “ten”) + σῠλλᾰβή (sŭllăbḗ, “syllable”). By surface analysis, deca- + sillabo.
From Late Latin diaphorēticus, from Ancient Greek διαφορητικός (diaphorētikós), from δῐᾰφόρησῐς (dĭăphórēsĭs).

From Late Latin diamantem, from Latin adamantem, from Ancient Greek ἀδάμας (adámas, “invincible, untamed; hard substance”), from ἀ- (a-, “un-”) + δαμάζω (damázō, “to overpower, tame, conquer”), from Proto-Indo-European *demh₂-.
Borrowed from Late Latin diarrhoea, from Ancient Greek διάρροια (diárrhoia, “through-flowing”), from διά (diá, “through”) + ῥέω (rhéō, “I flow”).
From Late Latin, from Ancient Greek διάστημα (diástēma).
From Late Latin diaeresis, from Ancient Greek δῐαίρεσῐς (dĭaíresĭs).
Borrowed from Late Latin diiambus, from Ancient Greek διίαμβος (diíambos), derived from δι- (di-, “two”) + ἴαμβος (íambos, “iambus”).
Borrowed from Late Latin Dionȳsiacus, from Ancient Greek Διονυσιακός (Dionusiakós), from Δῐόνῡσος (Dĭónūsos, “Dionysus”) + -ακός (-akós).
From Late Latin diptychum, from Ancient Greek δίπτυχος (díptukhos, “folded, doubled”), from δι- (di-) + πτυχή (ptukhḗ, “fold, layer”).
Borrowed from Late Latin diphthongus, from Ancient Greek δίφθογγος (díphthongos).
Borrowed from Late Latin hebdomada, from Latin hebdomas, from Ancient Greek ἑβδομάς (hebdomás), derived from ἕβδομος (hébdomos, “seventh”), derived from ἑπτά (heptá, “seven”).
From Late Latin ephemĕrus, from Ancient Greek ἐφήμερος (ephḗmeros, “lasting one day, short-lived”), from ἐπί (epí, “on”) + ἡμέρα (hēméra, “day”).

Learned borrowing from Late Latin eleēmosyna, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐλεημοσύνη (eleēmosúnē), from ἐλεήμων (eleḗmōn, “pitiful, merciful”) + -σῠ́νη (-sŭ́nē). Compare the inherited counterpart limosina, now archaic.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin hemicyclus, from Ancient Greek ἡμι- (hēmi-) + κύκλος (kúklos). By surface analysis, emi- + ciclo.
Borrowed from Late Latin hēmicrānia, from Ancient Greek ἡμικρᾱνίᾰ (hēmikrāníă). Doublet of micragna.
Borrowed from Late Latin encōmium, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐγκώμιον (enkṓmion), neuter form of ἐγκώμιος (enkṓmios), from ἐν (en, “in”) + κῶμος (kômos, “festival, revel”).

parole.significato: ennead (grouping or system containing nine objects)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin enneas, from Ancient Greek ἐννεάς (enneás), derived from ἐννέα (ennéa, “nine”).
From Late Latin entelechia, from Ancient Greek ἐντελέχεια (entelékheia), coined by Aristotle.

From Late Latin aeōnem (“age, eternity”), from Ancient Greek αἰών (aiṓn), from earlier αἰϝών (aiwṓn), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂oy-u-Hō, derived from *h₂óyu (“long time; lifetime”), derived from the root *h₂ey- (“vital force, life, age, eternity”).
Inherited from Late Latin hēpar (“liver”), from Ancient Greek ἧπαρ (hêpar, “liver”), from Proto-Hellenic *yékʷər, from Proto-Indo-European *yókʷr̥ (“liver”), derived from the root *Hyekʷ-.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin epicy̆clus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίκυκλος (epíkuklos). By surface analysis, epi- + ciclo.

From Late Latin epiglottidem, from Ancient Greek ἐπιγλωττίς (epiglōttís) derived from γλῶττα (glôtta), variant of γλῶσσα (glôssa, “tongue”). By surface analysis, epi- (“above”, “over”) + glottide (“glottis”).
From Late Latin epistola, from Ancient Greek ἐπιστολή (epistolḗ).
From Late Latin epitaphium, from Ancient Greek ἐπιτάφιος (epitáphios, “relating to a funeral”).
Borrowed from Late Latin epithesis, from Ancient Greek ἐπίθεσις (epíthesis).
With a change in ending, from Late Latin epopta, epoptēs, from Ancient Greek ἐπόπτης (epóptēs).
From Late Latin erēmus, Ancient Greek ἐρῆμος (erêmos)/ἔρημος (lonely, solitary, desert, waste). Doublet of ermo.
From Late Latin eremus, erēmus, from Ancient Greek ἔρημος (érēmos, “lonely, solitary, desert, waste”), with preservation of Greek accent over vowel length. Doublet of eremo.
From Late Latin hexagōnum, from Ancient Greek ἕξάγωνον (héxágōnon), from ἕξάγωνος (héxágōnos, “six-angled”).
Borrowed from Late Latin eschara (“scar, scab”), from Ancient Greek ἐσχάρα (eskhára, “hearth, brazier, scab”).
From Late Latin exorcizāre, from Ancient Greek ἐξορκίζειν (exorkízein, “banish an evil spirit; bind by oath”).
Borrowed from Late Latin esōtericus, from Ancient Greek ἐσωτερικός (esōterikós).
Borrowed from Late Latin exōtericus, from Ancient Greek ἐξωτερικός (exōterikós).
From Late Latin ethica, from Ancient Greek ἠθική (ēthikḗ), from ἠθικός (ēthikós, “of or for morals, moral, expressing character”), from ἦθος (êthos, “character, moral nature”).
From Late Latin hecticus, from Ancient Greek ἑκτικός (hektikós).
Borrowed from Late Latin ethnicus, from Ancient Greek ἐθνῐκός (ethnĭkós).

parole.significato: to preach the Gospel, to evangelize
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin evangelizāre, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγελίζω (euangelízō).
Late Latin famfalūca, from Ancient Greek πομφόλυξ (pomphólux, “air bubble”). Cf. Old French fanfalue (“trifle”), French fanfreluche (“frill”).
Borrowed from Late Latin phantasticus (“imaginary”), from Ancient Greek φανταστικός (phantastikós).
From Late Latin Pharaōnem (“pharaoh”), from Ancient Greek Φαραώ (Pharaṓ), from Hebrew פַּרְעֹה (par‘ōh), from Egyptian pr:aA (pr-ꜥꜣ, “palace”, “pharaoh”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin phaenomenon, from Ancient Greek φαινόμενον (phainómenon, “thing appearing to view”).
From Late Latin philanthrōpia, from Ancient Greek φιλανθρωπία (philanthrōpía).
From Late Latin phlegma, from Ancient Greek φλέγμα (phlégma, “flame; phlegm”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin phrasis (“diction”), from Ancient Greek φράσις (phrásis, “manner of expression”).
Inherited from Late Latin gamba. Cognate with Sicilian gamma ~ jamma.
Inherited from Late Latin ganathus, from Ancient Greek γνάθος (gnáthos).

parole.significato: the treasury in the temple of Jerusalem
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin gazophylacium, from Ancient Greek γαζοφυλάκιον (gazophulákion).
From Late Latin zēlōsus, from zēlus, from Ancient Greek ζῆλος (zêlos, “zeal, jealousy”), from ζηλόω (zēlóō, “to emulate, to be jealous”). Compare Spanish celoso, French jaloux.
From Late Latin genealogia, from Ancient Greek γενεαλογία (genealogía), from γενεά (geneá, “generation, descent”) and -λογία (-logía, “study of”).
Borrowed from Late Latin iūdaismus, from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαϊσμός (Ioudaïsmós).
From Late Latin gumma, from Latin cummi, gummi, from Ancient Greek κόμμι (kómmi).

parole.significato: vernacular (the language of a people or a national language)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin idioma, from Ancient Greek ἰδίωμα (idíōma, “peculiarity; idiom”).
Haplology from Late Latin īdōlolatrēs, from Ancient Greek εἰδωλολᾰ́τρης (eidōlolắtrēs).
Borrowed from Late Latin hydromantis, from Ancient Greek ὑδρόμαντις (hudrómantis), from ὑδρο- (hudro-, “hydro-, water”) + μάντις (mántis, “seer, prophet”). By surface analysis, idro- + -mante.
From Late Latin encaustum, from Ancient Greek ἔγκαυστον (énkauston). Compare French encre.

parole.significato: to use, wear, or open for the first time; to inaugurate
parole.testo: Late Latin encaeniare (“to consecrate, inaugurate”), from Ancient Greek ἐγκαίνια (enkaínia, “feast of dedication”), from Ancient Greek καινός (kainós, “new”).
From Late Latin hymnodicus, from Ancient Greek ὑμνῳδικός (humnōidikós).
Borrowed from Late Latin hypnōticus (“pertaining to sleep”), from Ancient Greek ὑπνωτικός (hupnōtikós, “sleep-inducing”, “soporific”).
From Late Latin hyposcenium, in turn from Ancient Greek ὑπό (hupó, “under”) + σκηνή (skēnḗ, “stage”).
Borrowed from Late Latin hypothetĭcus, from Ancient Greek ὑποθετικός (hupothetikós).

From Late Latin hippocampus, from Ancient Greek ἱππόκαμπος (hippókampos, from ῐ̔́ππος (hĭ́ppos, “horse”) + κάμπος (kámpos, “sea-monster”)). The anatomy sense is so named from its resemblance to the seahorse. By surface analysis, hippo- + campus.
Borrowed from Late Latin īrōnicus, from Ancient Greek εἰρωνικός (eirōnikós).

parole.significato: ithyphallic (of or pertaining to the erect phallus carried in bacchic processions)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin ithyphallicus, from Ancient Greek ἰθυφαλλικός (ithuphallikós), derived from ῑ̓θῠ́φαλλος (īthŭ́phallos, “phallus carried in festivals of Bacchus; ode sung in honour of the phallus; dance accompanying such an ode; dancer performing such a dance”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós, “of,
From Late Latin lēthargia, from Ancient Greek ληθαργία (lēthargía, “drowsiness”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin lītotēs, from Ancient Greek λιτότης (litótēs).

Borrowed from Late Latin logica, from Ancient Greek λογική (logikḗ, “logic”), from the feminine form of λογικός (logikós, “of or pertaining to speech or reason or reasoning, rational, reasonable”), from λόγος (lógos, “speech, reason”).
Borrowed from Late Latin logisticus, from Ancient Greek λογιστικός (logistikós).

Inherited from Late Latin māchināre (“mill, grind”), a verb based on Latin māchina (“device, mill”), an early borrowing from Ancient Greek. Compare Venetan masnar~maxenar, Friulian masanâ, Dalmatian macnur. Morphological doublet of macchinare, a borrowing from Latin.
From Late Latin magia, from Ancient Greek μαγεία (mageía).
Borrowed from Late Latin melancholia, from Ancient Greek μελαγχολία (melankholía, “blackness of the bile”) after the humorism theory.
From Late Latin pandura, from Ancient Greek πανδοῦρα (pandoûra), a Pre-Greek/substrate loan.
Borrowed from Late Latin maniacus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek μανιακός (maniakós), adjectival form of μανία (manía, “madness”).
From Late Latin manna, from Ancient Greek μάννα (mánna), from Hebrew מן (mān, “'manna”).
Borrowed from Late Latin metoecus, from Ancient Greek μέτοικος (métoikos), from μετα- (meta-) + οἶκος (oîkos, “house”).
From Late Latin metonymia, from Ancient Greek μετωνυμίᾱ (metōnumíā, “change of name”), from μετά (metá, “other”) + ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”).
Through a jocular transfer of sense, from Late Latin hēmicrānia (“migraine”), from Ancient Greek ἡμικρᾱνίᾰ (hēmikrāníă). Doublet of emicrania.
Inherited from Late Latin monachus.
Borrowed from Late Latin monarcha, from Ancient Greek μονάρχης (monárkhēs), variant of μόναρχος (mónarkhos, “sole ruler”).
From Late Latin monarchia, from Ancient Greek μοναρχία (monarkhía). By surface analysis, mono- (“one”, “only”) + -archia (“rule”, “command”).
From Late Latin necrōsis, from Ancient Greek νέκρωσις (nékrōsis). By surface analysis, necro- (“necro-”, “death”) + -osi (“-osis”, suffix denoting a medical condition).
Inherited from Late Latin naulum (“fare”), from Ancient Greek ναῦλος (naûlos, “a passenger's fee”), from ναῦς (naûs, “ship”).
Borrowed from Late Latin nosocomīum, from Ancient Greek νοσοκομεῖον (nosokomeîon, “hospital”), from νόσος (nósos, “disease, illness”) + κομέω (koméō, “to take care of”).
From Late Latin Oasis, from Ancient Greek Ὄασις (Óasis), from Demotic Egyptian wḥj, from Egyptian w-H-A-t:N25 (wḥꜣt, “the Oasis region; oasis”).
From Late Latin oidium, from Ancient Greek ᾠόν (ōión, “egg”).
Borrowed from Late Latin oligarcha, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγάρχης (oligárkhēs). By surface analysis, oligo- (“few”) + -arca (“ruler, leader”).
From Late Latin oligarchia, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγαρχία (oligarkhía). By surface analysis, oligo- (“few”) + -archia (“rule”, “government”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin oligarchicus, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγαρχικός (oligarkhikós). By surface analysis, oligarca (“oligarch”) + -ico (“-ic”, adjective-forming suffix).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin homileticus, from Ancient Greek ὁμιλητικός (homilētikós, “pertaining to conversation”), derived from ὁμιλέω (homiléō).
From Late Latin orphanus, from Ancient Greek ὀρφανός (orphanós, “without parents, fatherless”).

Inherited from Late Latin osma (in glosses) (or through a Vulgar Latin form *orma), from Ancient Greek ὀδμή (odmḗ, “odour, stench”). Compare Logudorian Sardinian orma, ormina, Romanian urmă, Aromanian urmã, Istriot urma, Friulian olme, Venetan usma, Neapolitan uoseme, Spanish husmo, Galician osmar,
Borrowed from Late Latin hōroscopicus, from Ancient Greek ὡροσκοπικός (hōroskopikós).
Borrowed from Late Latin orthodoxia, from Ancient Greek ὀρθοδοξία (orthodoxía, “right opinion”). By surface analysis, ortodosso + -ia

Borrowed from Late Latin optātīvus [modus] (a calque of Ancient Greek εὐκτική [ἔγκλισις] (euktikḗ [énklisis])), derived from Classical Latin optātus, past participle of optō (“to choose; to wish for”).
Borrowed from Late Latin parabola, from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ). Doublet of parola, which was inherited. Mathematical sense taken from New Latin or Greek.
From Late Latin paradīgma, from Ancient Greek παράδειγμα (parádeigma).
From Late Latin paragōgē, from Ancient Greek παραγωγή (paragōgḗ, “derivation, addition”).
From Late Latin paralogismus, from Ancient Greek παραλογισμός (paralogismós).

parole.significato: the Friday before the Jewish sabbath
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin parasceue, from Ancient Greek παρασκευή (paraskeuḗ, “preparazione”).
From Late Latin parenthesis, from Ancient Greek πᾰρένθεσῐς (părénthesĭs).
From Late Latin parochia, from Ancient Greek παροικία (paroikía, “a dwelling abroad”).
Inherited from Late Latin pasta, from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá).
From Late Latin epitaphium (“eulogy”), from Ancient Greek ἐπιτάφιος (epitáphios, “funereal”).

Borrowed from Late Latin pathēticus, from Ancient Greek παθητικός (pathētikós, “subject to feeling, capable of feeling, impassioned”), from παθητός (pathētós, “one who has suffered, subject to suffering”), from πάσχω (páskhō, “to suffer”).
From Late Latin pentagonum, from Ancient Greek πεντάγωνον (pentágōnon), from πεντάγωνος (pentágōnos, “five-angled”).
Borrowed from Late Latin pentarchia, from Ancient Greek πενταρχίᾱ (pentarkhíā), from πεντα- (penta-, “penta-, five”) + -αρχίᾱ (-arkhíā, “-archy, rule”). By surface analysis, penta- + -archia.
From Late Latin pentasyllabus, from Ancient Greek πεντασύλλαβος (pentasúllabos). By surface analysis, penta- + sillabo.
From Late Latin pergamēna.
From Late Latin pīganum, alternative form of pēganum (“rue”), ultimately from Ancient Greek πήγανον (pḗganon).
Borrowed from Late Latin pleonasmus, from Ancient Greek πλεονασμός (pleonasmós), from πλεονάζω (pleonázō, “I am superfluous”), from πλείων (pleíōn, “more”).
From Late Latin polygamia, from Ancient Greek πολυγαμία (polugamía).

parole.significato: polygon (plane figure bounded by straight edges)
parole.testo: From Late Latin polygōnum, from Ancient Greek πολύγωνον (polúgōnon).
From [Teucrium] polium, from Late Latin polium, polion, from Ancient Greek πόλιον (pólion), from πολιός (poliós, “white, grey”).
From Late Latin polītīa, from Ancient Greek πολιτεία (politeía).

From Late Latin practicus, from Ancient Greek πρᾱκτῐκός (prāktĭkós, “pertaining to an action”), derived from πρᾱγ- (prāg-), the root of πρᾱ́σσω (prā́ssō, “to do”) + -τῐκός (-tĭkós, verbal adjective suffix).
From Late Latin presbyter, from Ancient Greek πρεσβύτερος (presbúteros), from πρέσβυς (présbus, “elder, older”).
Borrowed from Late Latin prisma, from Ancient Greek πρίσμα (prísma), from πρίω (príō, “to saw”).
Borrowed from Late Latin problematicus, from Ancient Greek προβληματικός (problēmatikós), from πρόβλημα (próblēma, “outjutting, barrier, problem”).

parole.significato: a staircase that leads to the entrance of a building
parole.testo: From Late Latin proferulum, itself from Ancient Greek προφερής (propherḗs) + -ulum.
From Late Latin programma, from Ancient Greek πρόγραμμα (prógramma).
From Late Latin prosēlytus, from Ancient Greek προσήλυτος (prosḗlutos).
Borrowed from Late Latin prosthesis, from Ancient Greek πρόσθεσῐς (prósthesĭs), which was confused with Late Latin prothesis from Ancient Greek πρόθεσις (próthesis).
Borrowed from Late Latin protasis, from Ancient Greek πρότασις (prótasis).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin ptarmicus, from Ancient Greek πταρμικός (ptarmikós), derived from πταρμός (ptarmós, “sneeze”).
From Late Latin rabbī, from Ancient Greek ῥαββί (rhabbí, literally “O my Master”), from Hebrew רבי (rabbī, “rabbi”, “spiritual teacher”).
From Late Latin, from Ancient Greek ῥαφή (rhaphḗ, “seam”).
From Late Latin oryza, from Ancient Greek ὄρυζα (óruza).
From the vulgarisation of Late Latin erēmīta, from Ancient Greek ἐρημίτης (erēmítēs). Doublet of eremita. Compare Sicilian rimitu.
From Late Latin ōs sacrum, calque of Ancient Greek ἱερὸν ὀστέον (hieròn ostéon, “big bone”), with influence from ἱερός (hierós, “sacred”).
From Late Latin sauma, from Latin sagma, from Ancient Greek σάγμα (ságma). Compare the doublet soma (“load, burden”).
From Late Latin psalmus, from Ancient Greek ψαλμός (psalmós, “song sung to a harp, performance on a stringed instrument”), from ψάλλω (psállō, “to pluck an instrument”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin psalmōdia, from Ancient Greek ψαλμῳδία (psalmōidía, “singing to a harp”), from ψαλμός (psalmós) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”).
Via Late Latin Saracenus from Ancient Greek Σαρακηνός (Sarakēnós).
From Late Latin sarcasmus, from Ancient Greek σαρκασμός (sarkasmós).
From Late Latin satyriasis, from Ancient Greek σατυρίασις (saturíasis).
Inherited from Late Latin scaphus, from Ancient Greek σκάφος (skáphos, “hull”).
Borrowed from Late Latin scalēnus, from Ancient Greek σκᾰληνός (skălēnós, “uneven, unequal, scalene”).
Perhaps from Late Latin scarificāre, from Latin scarifāre (“to scarify”), from Ancient Greek σκαριφάομαι (skaripháomai, “to scratch an outline”). Compare French scarifier (“to scarify”).
From Late Latin scarificāre, from Latin scarifāre (“to scarify”), from Ancient Greek σκαριφᾶσθαι (skariphâsthai, “to scratch an outline”), from σκάριφος (skáriphos, “writing, drawing, sketching”).
From Late Latin sciaticus, variant of ischiadicus, from Ancient Greek ἰσχιαδικός (iskhiadikós), the adjective of ἰσχίον (iskhíon, “hip”). Doublet of ischiatico.
From Late Latin scopus (“target”).

From Late Latin scrōfulae, derived from scrōfa (“sow, female pig”) as a semantic calque of Ancient Greek χοιράδες (khoirádes), derived from χοῖρος (khoîros, “young pig”), because the scars associated with the pathology were deemed reminiscent of a pathology found in pigs.
Borrowed from Late Latin sphēra, from Latin sphaera (“ball, globe, celestial sphere”), from Ancient Greek σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “ball, globe”).
From Late Latin sympathīa, from Ancient Greek συμπάθεια (sumpátheia).
From Late Latin synagōga, from Ancient Greek συναγωγή (sunagōgḗ, “assembly”).
Borrowed from Late Latin syncope, from Ancient Greek συγκοπή (sunkopḗ), from σύν (sún) + κόπτω (kóptō, “strike, cut off”).
From Late Latin synonymĭa, from Ancient Greek συνωνυμία (sunōnumía). By surface analysis, sinonimo + -ia.
From Late Latin synōnymum, from Ancient Greek συνώνυμος (sunṓnumos). By surface analysis, sin- + -o- + -nimo.
From Late Latin sirēna, from Latin Sīrēn, from Ancient Greek Σειρήν (Seirḗn). Cognate with Piedmontese siren-a.
From Late Latin systēma, from Ancient Greek σύστημα (sústēma).

parole.significato: the load borne by a pack animal
parole.testo: From Late Latin sauma, from alteration of Latin sagma, from Ancient Greek σάγμα (ságma). Compare the doublet salma (“corpse”). Cognate to French somme (“packsaddle”).

From Late Latin sagmārius, saumārius, salmārius, from Late Latin sagma (“pack saddle”), from Ancient Greek σάγμα (ságma). Doublet of somiere. The obsolete English word summer (“pack-horse”) is borrowed from the same source.
Borrowed from Late Latin spermatĭcus, from Ancient Greek σπερματικός (spermatikós). By surface analysis, sperma + -atico.
Borrowed from Late Latin stypsis, from Ancient Greek στῦψις (stûpsis), from στύφω (stúphō).
From Late Latin stolus, from Ancient Greek στόλος (stólos, “fleet, army”).
Via Late Latin tarantula from Ancient Greek and ultimately Illyrian.
Borrowed from Late Latin theticus, from Ancient Greek θετικός (thetikós).
Borrowed from Late Latin tetrameter, tetrametrus, from Ancient Greek τετρᾰ́μετρος (tetrắmetros). By surface analysis, tetra- + -metro.
From Late Latin tetrarcha, from Latin tetrarchēs, from Ancient Greek τετράρχης (tetrárkhēs). By surface analysis, tetra- + -arca.
From Late Latin tetrarchia, from Ancient Greek. By surface analysis, tetra- + -archia.
From Late Latin tumba, from Ancient Greek τύμβος (túmbos).
From Late Latin tunnus, from Latin thunnus, thynnus, from Ancient Greek θύννος (thúnnos).
Borrowed from Late Latin topicus, from Ancient Greek τοπῐκός (topĭkós), from τόπος (tópos).
From Late Latin trepanum, from Ancient Greek τρύπανον (trúpanon, “auger, borer”).
From Late Latin trapezium, from Ancient Greek τραπέζιον (trapézion).
From Late Latin trophaeum, variant of Latin tropaeum (“trophy, victory memorial”), from Ancient Greek τρόπαιον (trópaion), from τροπή (tropḗ, “turning, trope”), from τρέπω (trépō, “to turn”).
Borrowed from Late Latin tropologicus, from Ancient Greek τροπολογικός (tropologikós).
From Late Latin tructa, possibly from Ancient Greek τρώκτης (trṓktēs).
Borrowed from Late Latin xenodochīum, from Ancient Greek ξενοδοχεῖον (xenodokheîon).
From Late Latin sapphīrus, from Ancient Greek σάπφειρος (sáppheiros, “lapis lazuli”).
From Late Latin gingiber, Latin zingiberī.
From Late Latin zeugma, from Ancient Greek ζεῦγμα (zeûgma, “bond; yoking”).
From Late Latin thia, from Ancient Greek θεία (theía).
Inherited from Late Latin thius, from Ancient Greek θεῖος (theîos). Compare Spanish tío, Portuguese tio, Sicilian ziu, Sardinian tiu or tziu, Venetan sio.
